context: tank & dispenser commissioning-led · environmental containment critical

brief.intro: A fuel or service station is a small building wrapped around a much bigger buried risk: underground storage tanks holding petrol or diesel, feeding dispensers under a canopy. New to this type? The schedule is not about the retail shop or canopy structure — it is about safely installing, testing and certifying the tanks, pipework and vapour-recovery/leak-detection systems that prevent fuel escaping into the ground and the air. Environmental and fire-authority approvals gate almost every stage, from tank delivery to first fuel-in. The retail building and canopy can be built in parallel, but the station cannot open until the fuel system has passed its tightness and calibration tests.

scope.name: Site enabling & environmental controls
scope.desc: Spill containment during excavation and groundwater monitoring where required.

scope.name: Tank pit excavation & installation
scope.desc: Deep excavation, tank bedding, and setting and anchoring the underground storage tanks (USTs).

scope.name: Tank pit backfill & containment
scope.desc: Secondary containment, interstitial monitoring and compacted backfill around the tanks.

scope.name: Fuel pipework & dispensers
scope.desc: Product piping, vapour-recovery piping and dispenser islands.

scope.name: Forecourt & canopy
scope.desc: Canopy structure and forecourt slab with falls to the interceptor and spill containment.

scope.name: Retail building & shop fit-out
scope.desc: The associated convenience store or kiosk.

scope.name: Fire protection
scope.desc: Fire suppression at the dispensers and hydrants/extinguishers where required.

scope.name: Electrical & fuel-management systems
scope.desc: Power to dispensers and canopy, point-of-sale, and tank-gauging/leak-detection electronics.

scope.name: Testing, calibration & tightness testing
scope.desc: Tank/pipework tightness test, dispenser calibration and vapour-recovery test.

scope.name: Environmental sign-off & commissioning
scope.desc: Fire-authority and environmental-authority approval, then first fuel-in.

glossary.plain: underground storage tank — the buried tank holding the fuel.
a pressure/vacuum test proving the tank and pipework have no leaks before fuel is introduced.
sensors in the space between a tank's inner and outer wall that detect a leak before it reaches the ground.
piping and equipment that capture fuel vapour during delivery and dispensing instead of releasing it to air.
the paved area under the canopy where vehicles fuel up.
an underground chamber that separates fuel/oil from surface water before it drains away.
proving a dispenser measures and charges for the exact volume of fuel delivered.
an outer barrier — a double-wall tank or a lined pit — that catches any leak from the primary tank or pipe.

must_get_right: Treat the tank pit and pipework as the critical path, not the retail building — nothing opens until the fuel system passes its tightness test and gets fire/environmental sign-off.
Secure environmental and fire-authority approvals early — tank delivery, backfill and first fuel-in are usually each gated by a separate inspection or permit.
Never backfill or cover pipework before the tightness test is witnessed and passed — a failure discovered after backfill means re-excavation.
Coordinate the interceptor and forecourt falls with the paving programme — retrofitting drainage after the slab is poured is expensive and slow.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress; calculated by F9 with total float kept ≥ 0 in the baseline. Given the compact scope, the tank/pipework sequence is modelled activity-by-activity rather than as a single summary bar.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and tank works run a standard 6-day week; testing (tightness test, calibration) is scheduled around inspector availability and may hold the calendar for a witnessed test rather than a fixed duration.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs tank-pit excavation → tank set & containment → backfill → pipework → dispenser install → tightness test → calibration → environmental/fire-authority sign-off → first fuel-in. The retail building and canopy run in parallel and rarely govern the finish date.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Environmental and fire-authority permits are obtained per phase gate (excavation, tank delivery, first fuel-in); groundwater and ground conditions are as per the site investigation; a single fuel supplier delivers to a confirmed programme.

sections.body: Tanks and dispensing equipment are tracked as milestones and typically drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: The tank pit needs a large, clear excavation and crane access for tank set; if the station stays open to traffic during works, phased excavation and temporary access are needed. Hazardous-area (ATEX) certified trades are a resource constraint for the electrical and pipework scope.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: a failed tightness test discovered after backfill, groundwater or contaminated-ground conditions differing from the site investigation, and permit delays gating tank delivery or first fuel-in. Contingency is held before backfill and before the tightness test.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1–2 to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4 for tank-pit and pipework sequencing on site — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
